summary:
No departmental trans statute, ordinance, enforcement action or incident series specific to Junín appears in the inventory. Junín therefore stands under Peru's national framework, and the national assessment governs what a trans visitor to the department should expect to face.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity. The national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The restroom restriction moved through Congress in two stages. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. The draft carried exceptions for custody situations, where medical attention is required, or when accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and banned 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions. A legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of IDEHPUCP, the human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, states that the provision violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The same April 2025 legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

In practice the restriction places restroom access in the hands of security staff. LGBTI activist Gianna Camacho, who calls the measure discriminatory, warns that access will depend on staff's personal judgment, including identity checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

The restriction reaches private and commercial premises as well as state facilities. A national consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

IDEHPUCP has also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu, and found that the bathroom provision discriminates openly against trans and non-binary people by barring them from facilities matching their gender identity while implicitly framing them as harassment risks. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, published in July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023. Trans women were more than half the homicide victims at 30, followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, of whom 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty including multiple gunshots and stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denunciations logged in 2020. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, was abducted by a gang in central Lima and killed in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. Report co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stresses that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The national restroom ban sits alongside a wider regional trajectory. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard the April 2025 article 5 runs against on the reading advanced by IDEHPUCP.

Two protective developments are on record and cut against the direction of the 2025 legislation. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
localsOnly:
Residents of Junín live under the same national restroom rule as visitors, but enforcement incidents recorded in the inventory come from Lima rather than the department: a consumer-protection body's dismissal of a trans woman's complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and the on-air harassment of congresswoman Susel Paredes by presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV.

Peru's health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance in June 2024, which affects how trans patients are treated in healthcare settings, including in Junín's facilities.

In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, acting on an activist legal challenge, struck down an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional, establishing a route that residents can use against discriminatory measures.

Hate-crime and violence figures for Peru are collected nationally by the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI; the 2024 report logged 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases for 2020-2023, and co-author Gianna Camacho states the published figures are only a sub-registry.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Junín-specific enforcement finding, arrest, prosecution or documented incident involving a trans person appears in the inventory; whether article 5 has been applied in the department, and by which authority, is unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory does not state whether Junín has its own departmental or municipal anti-discrimination instrument, or whether Huancayo or other municipalities in the department have adopted signage or facility rules of their own. This is not sourced either way.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans travellers, including recognition of gender markers on passports, are not covered by the inventory and remain unresolved for this record.

The inventory does not indicate whether the July 2025 constitutional court ruling applies nationally or only within the court's territorial jurisdiction, nor whether it has been appealed.
